title: CDN (Content Delivery Network): caches static content (images, CSS, JS, video) at edge servers close to users, reduces latency and origin server load.
keyPoints: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of edge servers that cache static content close to users for low-latency delivery.
On a cache miss the edge fetches from the origin once, stores it, and serves all subsequent requests until the TTL expires.
The cache key (usually the URL) decides what counts as the same object; incorrect keys can leak personalized content.
Versioned URLs (logo-v2.png) are preferred over explicit invalidation because purging is slow and costly.
Only cache content identical for every user; dynamic personalized content must stay off the edge or use per-user cache keys.
Signed, time-limited URLs protect private or premium content so only authorized users can fetch it.
CDNs also provide DDoS absorption and API acceleration by routing through optimized backbone networks.

s1_definition.oneliner: Cache static content at edge servers near users so it loads fast and the origin is spared, controlling freshness with TTL and invalidation.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** : a geographically distributed network of edge servers that cache static and cacheable content close to end users.
- **Edge server** : a CDN node in a specific geographic region that serves cached content to nearby users.
- **TTL (time-to-live)** : the duration an object stays cached at an edge before it must be re-fetched from the origin.
- **Cache key** : the identifier (usually the URL) that determines what counts as the same cached object.
- **Invalidation** : removing stale content from the edge before the TTL expires, either by explicit purge or versioned URLs.
- **Signed URL** : a time-limited, tamper-proof link that restricts access to authorized users.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India's main data centre is in one city, but customers are everywhere. If Rajesh in Bengaluru downloads the bank's app logo and statement PDFs from that one distant data centre every time, it is slow and overloads the centre. Instead the bank keeps copies of these unchanging files in small storage rooms in every city. Rajesh gets the logo from the Bengaluru room instantly, and the main data centre barely notices. Those local storage rooms are CDN edge servers.

  ┌──────────┐                              ┌──────────────┐

                            ▼                      │
                    ┌───────────────┐               │
                    │  Edge Server  │  2. Cache HIT │
                    │   (Mumbai)    │  -> serve      │
                    │               │  instantly     │
                    │  Cache MISS:  │               │
                    │  fetch from   │───────────────┘
                    │  origin once  │  3. Store + serve
                    └───────────────┘

  ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐
  │ Edge Delhi │    │ Edge Mumbai│    │ Edge B'lore│
  │  HIT: 0ms │    │  HIT: 0ms  │    │  HIT: 0ms  │
  │ MISS: 5ms │    │ MISS: 50ms │    │ MISS: 80ms │
  │ (nearby)   │    │ (medium)   │    │ (far)      │
  └────────────┘    └────────────┘    └────────────┘

  What to cache:  images, CSS, JS, fonts, video segments
  What NOT to cache: account balances, personalized data

sections.s6_takeaway:
A content delivery network is a geographically distributed set of edge servers that cache static, cacheable content close to end users, so a request is served from a nearby edge instead of the distant origin. The fundamental benefit is proximity: serving a file from an edge a few milliseconds away rather than an origin hundreds of milliseconds away makes an app feel instant, while simultaneously sparing the origin and cutting bandwidth cost.

The mechanism is caching with a TTL. When an edge lacks a requested file, it fetches it from the origin once, stores it, and serves all subsequent requests from its cache until the TTL expires. That is why origin load drops so dramatically. At National Bank of India, this is exactly what fixed slow app loads for distant customers, because the logo, stylesheet, and help images came from a nearby edge rather than the central data centre.

Keeping content fresh is the next concern. The cache key, usually the URL, decides what counts as the same object, and I am careful never to let a cache key accidentally serve one user's personalized content to another. When a file changes, I prefer versioned URLs, giving the updated file a new name so clients simply request a fresh, uncached object, which avoids the delay and cost of purging. Crucially, I only cache content identical for every user and keep dynamic personalized content such as account balances off the edge entirely.

The senior points I always raise are security and resilience. Premium or private content is protected with signed, time-limited URLs so only authorized users can fetch it, which matters for a bank serving confidential documents. And because the CDN's distributed edge network can absorb volumetric traffic far better than a single origin, it doubles as DDoS protection and even accelerates API traffic through optimized backbone routing.

Remember one sentence: a CDN caches static content at the edge for speed, uses versioned URLs for freshness, signed URLs for security, and its distributed nature for DDoS resilience.
